Carlyle Group (NASDAQ:CG) expects its next U.S. buyout fund to reach an initial close this quarter or next, as the firm prepares for a busy fundraising cycle across private equity, credit and secondaries, Co-President and Head of Private Equity John Redett said.

Redett said he felt good about the prospects for the fundraise, although raising private equity capital remained more difficult than it was five years ago. The timing of a first close depends in part on when several large limited partners commit, he said.

His comments came as the firm pursues a previously discussed $200 billion fundraising target over three years. The operator said $40 billion of that target was expected to come from wealth channels.

Redett said Carlyle was returning capital globally at a rate closer to 18% of net asset value, compared with roughly 12% for the private equity industry. In the U.S., Carlyle's rate was above 20%, he said.

He attributed part of the difference to Carlyle's diversified portfolio and its avoidance of an excessive concentration in software investments. Industrywide, slower returns of capital have made it harder for some limited partners to allocate money to private equity, he said.

Redett acknowledged that Carlyle's CP VII fund had not met the firm's expectations, but said management had outlined a path forward to investors. He did not directly address the likelihood of the fund generating carried interest.

By contrast, he said CP VIII, which is 75% invested, was positioned to be a strong fund. "We do not have" one or two companies in the portfolio that raise the concerns typically seen at that stage, he said.

Carlyle is raising its first defense and industrial fund, focused on the U.S. and Europe, as well as a global energy fund. Redett said defense, energy, health care, financial services and industrials were areas of opportunity for the firm.

The defense fund will target more middle-market opportunities than Carlyle's large U.S. buyout fund, he said. Redett identified cybersecurity, data protection, shipbuilding and conventional defense capabilities as areas of interest. He said drones were less attractive because of the large number of manufacturers and the difficulty of identifying a sustainable platform.

Redett also said Carlyle had announced its first deal for the defense fund, Secturion, which provides encryption for data in transit.

Redett highlighted a structured transaction led by Carlyle's AlpInvest business that earmarked $5 billion for the current U.S. buyout vintage while providing liquidity to some fund investors. He said the response from limited partners was positive and that Carlyle was considering whether the structure could apply elsewhere.

AlpInvest's market data and relationships have become more closely integrated with Carlyle's investment businesses, he said. Redett also expects growth in credit secondaries, which he estimated at about $25 billion, compared with a $250 billion equity secondaries market.

In wealth management, Carlyle's private equity product, CPEP, recently crossed $1 billion, Redett said. It went live on its first wirehouse platform a couple of months ago, with additional platforms expected in 2027 and 2028. He cautioned that growth in private markets products for individual investors would take time, particularly amid recent bumps on the credit side.

Redett said he expects fundraising and asset growth to drive expansion in Carlyle's fee-related earnings margin toward 50% or higher. Automation could help at the margin, he said, but growth rather than cost efficiencies would be the principal driver.

In Europe, where Carlyle has faced buyout challenges, Redett said the firm had changed leadership and rebuilt the team. He estimated the transition was about 90% complete and noted that the latest European fund would be substantially smaller than its predecessor.

The Carlyle Group Inc is a global alternative asset manager that invests on behalf of institutional and individual clients. Its business includes private equity, credit and investment solutions, including portfolios of private equity funds and related investments.

Founded in Washington, DC, in 1987, Carlyle has grown into an international firm with investment activities and offices across North America, Europe and Asia, among other regions. Its strategies span a range of industries and markets, and it works with businesses at different stages of development.

Harvey Schwartz became Carlyle's chief executive officer in 2023.

Carlyle Group(NASDAQ:CG)의 공동 사장이자 사모펀드 책임자인 John Redett은 회사가 사모펀드, 신용 및 2차 채권 전반에 걸쳐 바쁜 자금 조달 주기를 준비하고 있기 때문에 이번 분기 또는 다음 분기에 차기 미국 매수 펀드가 초기 마감에 도달할 것으로 예상한다고 말했다.
Redett는 비록 사모펀드 조달이 5년 전보다 여전히 더 어려웠지만 자금 조달 전망에 대해 기분이 좋다고 말했다. 1차 클로즈 시기는 부분적으로 여러 대규모 유한 파트너가 약속하는 시기에 달려 있다고 그는 말했다.
그의 발언은 회사가 이전에 논의된 3년에 걸쳐 2000억 달러의 자금 조달 목표를 추구하는 가운데 나온 것이다. 운영자는 해당 목표 중 400억 달러가 자산 채널에서 나올 것으로 예상된다고 말했다.
Redett은 Carlyle이 전 세계적으로 순 자산 가치의 18%에 가까운 비율로 자본을 반환하고 있다고 밝혔는데, 이는 사모펀드 업계의 경우 약 12%에 해당한다. 미국에서는 Carlyle의 비율이 20%를 넘었다고 그는 말했다.
그는 그 차이의 일부를 Carlyle의 다각화된 포트폴리오와 소프트웨어 투자에 대한 지나친 집중을 피한 덕분이라고 생각했다. 업계 전반에 걸쳐 자본 수익률이 느려지면서 일부 유한 파트너가 사모펀드에 자금을 할당하는 것이 더 어려워졌다고 그는 말했다.
Redett는 Carlyle의 CP VII 펀드가 회사의 기대를 충족시키지 못했다는 점을 인정했지만 경영진이 투자자에게 앞으로 나아갈 길을 설명했다고 말했다. 그는 펀드가 이자를 창출할 가능성에 대해 직접적으로 언급하지 않았다.
반면 75%가 투자된 CP VIII는 강력한 펀드로 자리매김했다고 말했다. 그는 "우리는 포트폴리오에 해당 단계에서 일반적으로 나타나는 우려를 제기하는 회사가 한두 개 없다"고 말했다.
Carlyle은 미국과 유럽에 초점을 맞춘 최초의 국방 및 산업 기금과 글로벌 에너지 기금을 조성하고 있다. Redett은 국방, 에너지, 의료, 금융 서비스 및 산업 분야가 회사에 기회가 있는 분야라고 말했다.
그는 국방펀드가 Carlyle의 대규모 미국 매입 펀드보다 더 많은 중간 시장 기회를 목표로 삼을 것이라고 말했다. Redett은 사이버 보안, 데이터 보호, 조선 및 재래식 방어 역량을 관심 분야로 식별했다. 그는 제조업체 수가 많고 지속 가능한 플랫폼을 식별하기 어렵기 때문에 드론의 매력이 떨어진다고 말했다.
Redett는 또한 Carlyle이 전송 중인 데이터에 대한 암호화를 제공하는 국방 기금인 Seturion에 대한 첫 번째 거래를 발표했다고 말했다.
Redett은 일부 펀드 투자자에게 유동성을 제공하는 동시에 현재 미국 매수 빈티지에 50억 달러를 할당한 Carlyle의 AlpInvest 사업이 주도하는 구조화된 거래를 강조했다. 그는 LP(유한책임투자자)들의 반응이 긍정적이며 Carlyle이 구조가 다른 곳에 적용될 수 있는지 고려하고 있다고 말했다.
